planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wasabi arugula bolts and turns fiery hot quickly in summer heat, so plan for cool-season harvest and succession sow every two to three weeks.

directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wasabi arugula bolts and turns fiery hot quickly in summer heat, so plan for cool-season harvest and succession sow every two to three weeks. This selection of salad arugula is bred for an intense, sinus-clearing heat reminiscent of true wasabi, with deeply lobed, dark green leaves that pack noticeably more pungency than standard arugula, especially as plants mature or experience heat or drought stress. Harvest young leaves for a milder bite in mixed salads, or let plants grow larger for a bold, spicy addition to sandwiches and cooked greens where its heat mellows somewhat with cooking. Partial shade in warm climates helps delay bolting and keeps the intense flavor from becoming overwhelming; keep soil consistently moist to slow premature flowering.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Par-Cel is grown for its leaves rather than a blanched stalk and is much easier and faster to raise than standard stalk celery.

directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Par-Cel is grown for its leaves rather than a blanched stalk and is much easier and faster to raise than standard stalk celery. This cutting-type celery produces a bushy clump of thin, dark green, flat-leaf-parsley-like stems and foliage with full, concentrated celery flavor, cut and used as a seasoning herb rather than eaten as a crunchy stalk vegetable. It resists bolting and disease better than conventional celery, tolerates the light shade and humidity of a Gulf South summer far better than blanched celery, and regrows readily after cutting for a season-long harvest. Snip outer stems as needed for soups, stocks, and stuffing, always leaving the center growing point intact to keep the plant productive.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; purple mitsuba self-sows readily in a shaded herb bed once established and naturalizes as a woodland-edge perennial herb.

directions: Direct sow in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; purple mitsuba self-sows readily in a shaded herb bed once established and naturalizes as a woodland-edge perennial herb. This ornamental purple-leaved form of Japanese wild parsley (mitsuba) carries deep burgundy-purple, three-lobed leaves on slender stems, combining the same mild parsley-celery-anise flavor prized in Japanese cooking with striking, season-long foliage color for a shaded herb or ornamental border. Unlike most culinary herbs, it thrives in full shade and actually prefers it to hot sun, making it a useful flavor and color addition to the deep-shade parts of a garden where few edible herbs perform well. Harvest young leaves and stems continuously for soups, salads, and garnishes, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or late summer into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Lady holds its color and resists bolting better in the shorter days of fall than in the heat and long days of spring.

directions: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or late summer into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Lady holds its color and resists bolting better in the shorter days of fall than in the heat and long days of spring. Glossy, deep purple-black leaves top pale green petioles in a compact, upright rosette, giving this bok choy strong ornamental value alongside its mild, sweet, crisp flavor, and it holds its rich color whether cooked or eaten raw in salads. Bred as a hybrid for uniform heads and improved bolt resistance compared to open-pollinated purple pak choi types, it matures quickly enough for two full crops in a single spring-to-fall season in most climates. Harvest whole heads at full size or pick outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again harvest, and provide light afternoon shade to extend the harvest window into warmer weather.

common_name: Cupid's Shaving Brush (Ebolo, Yoruba Tassel Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cupid's shaving brush self-sows readily in warm, humid climates and is typically grown as a cut-and-come-again warm-season green.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cupid's shaving brush self-sows readily in warm, humid climates and is typically grown as a cut-and-come-again warm-season green. Known as ebolo in West African cooking, this fast-growing, weedy annual produces tender, slightly bitter, mineral-rich leaves used cooked in soups and stews much like a spinach substitute, along with small, tufted, magenta-pink brush-like flower heads that give the plant its whimsical common name. It tolerates the heat, humidity, and light shade of a Gulf South summer better than most temperate greens, continuing to produce through the hottest months when lettuce and spinach have long since bolted. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips regularly to keep plants productive and delay flowering, and expect volunteer seedlings the following season once it is established in a bed.
